title: How organisations buy, and where to spend your time

say: How organisations buy, and where to spend your time.
This is the video for module one of B2B Sales Strategy.
B2B means business to business. You sell to an organisation, like a company, school, hospital or NGO, not to one person for personal use.

say: Most organisations have a written rule on how much each manager may approve. It tells you who really signs.
For example, Amina's contact is the HR manager of a food company in Ota.
Her fee is 300,000 naira a month, so a one-year contract is 3,600,000 naira.
She asks how purchases this size are approved. The HR manager can approve up to 500,000 naira, and the finance controller up to 2,000,000.

say: So the managing director is the economic buyer, and the finance controller reviews the numbers first. Amina must prepare a business case they can defend, not just a demo for HR.

say: Ask about process, not power. Ask, how does a purchase like this usually get approved here? And, apart from you, who else will be involved?

say: Asking, are you the decision-maker, can embarrass people. And never go to the managing director behind your contact's back. Ask your contact to introduce you.

say: For example, Ifeoma runs a staff training business in Lagos. Her target is 18,000,000 naira of new contracts in 12 months, and her average deal is 1,500,000. So she needs 12 wins.
Her win rate on qualified opportunities is 25%. So she needs 12 divided by 0.25, which is 48 qualified opportunities.
That is 4 new qualified opportunities every month, about one a week.
With a 25% win rate she needs 4 times coverage: pipeline worth 4 times what she must close this quarter.
A qualified opportunity has a real need, a conversation with someone in the decision, and a realistic path to purchase. Counting unqualified names is the most common way sellers fool themselves.

panel.heading: Plan backwards from your target
panel.rule: Only count qualified opportunities, never every name you messaged.

say: An ideal customer profile describes the organisations that get the most value from you. Write down their sector, and the size measure that drives your price, like staff or beds.
Add the location you can serve well, and the situation, the problem they are likely to have.
And their ability to pay.
Then look for buying signals: a new branch, a new managing director, a new regulation, or a job advert for the very role you support.
For example, Halima sells IT support to private healthcare in Abuja. She scores each account from 1 to 5 on fit, signs of need, access and ability to pay.

panel.heading: Score and tier your list
items: Multiply by weights that add to 100%

say: Fit weighs 40%, need 30%, access and ability to pay 15% each.

panel.heading: Score and tier your list
items: Multiply by weights that add to 100%

say: Hospital B, opening a second branch, scores 4.55. Clinic E, advertising for an IT officer, scores 4.15. Both are Tier 1 and get personal effort this month.

items: Multiply by weights that add to 100%

say: Lab C and hospital D score 3.4, so they are Tier 2. Clinic A scores 2.7, Tier 3 for now. Keep Tier 1 short, and re-score every three months.

say: To remember. A group decides, so find each role. Approval limits show who really signs. Plan backwards from your target, with your own honest numbers. And a short, scored Tier 1 list beats a long generic one.

panel.heading: Remember
items: A group decides; find each role
Approval limits show who really signs
Target / deal size = wins; wins / win rate = opportunities
Use your own numbers and honest definitions
A short, scored Tier 1 list beats a long one
